title: Physical networks, Kubernetes networking and enterprise traffic paths

paras: From modem and router to cluster datapaths, ingress, CNI, CSI, load balancers and the access–distribution–core design.
Technical correction policy: detailed mechanisms, examples and verification in the corrections handbook

B011-P04: Kubernetes equivalents for modem, firewall, router, switch, server NIC, physical media, VLAN, LAG. B011-P05: storage-area-network adapters and the application delivery controller (ADC). B011-P06: guided and unguided media, ISP-to-Wi-Fi traffic chain and device responsibilities. B011-P07: ordered roles of modem/ONT, edge router, firewall, core, distribution, access, endpoints and application security.

Editorial method: each original analogy is retained as a hypothesis, followed by the closest real implementation and limits. A CNI is a plugin interface, not itself a cable; a Kubernetes Service is a virtual service abstraction, not an Ethernet switch.

ISP network / last-mile fiber, DSL, or cellular │ [ONT / modem / cellular gateway] — terminates provider access technology │ Ethernet or integrated interface [Edge router] — L3 forwarding, default route, BGP or static routing, optional NAT │ [Firewall / security zones] — policy, stateful inspection, DMZ boundaries │ [Core switch pair] — resilient high-capacity campus backbone │ [Distribution switches] — aggregation, routing boundaries, ACLs as designed │ [Access switches] — endpoints, VLAN membership, PoE, Wi-Fi AP uplinks ├── [Wi-Fi AP] )))) laptops and phones ├── [Server NIC / HBA] — compute or storage fabrics └── [Industrial gateway] — OT/IoT segmentation Important qualification: this is a teaching topology, not a required universal sequence. Real designs may collapse core and distribution, place firewalls in different positions, or combine ONT/router/firewall/AP into one appliance. A router does not necessarily perform NAT; NAT is an independent function. Fiber optics carry modulated light rather than requiring a classic analog telephone modem.

blocks.h2: 03 · ADC: network delivery, application delivery, and observability
paras: Your note correctly separates network traffic (packets, TCP/UDP) from application traffic (HTTP/HTTPS requests) and monitoring. An application delivery controller may terminate TLS, perform L4/L7 load balancing, health checks, persistence, request routing and sometimes WAF protections. Modern implementations include dedicated appliances, software reverse proxies and cloud managed load balancers.

Client HTTPS request → public listener / ADC → TLS termination (optional) → policy + routing + health-based backend selection → backend pool: app-A | app-B | app-C → response via ADC or configured return path Observability: metrics + logs + traces + health checks Correction: DPDK is a userspace packet-processing framework, not a universal requirement for ADCs. ADCs can be built on ordinary kernel networking; eBPF, DPDK, ASICs or SmartNICs are optional acceleration choices.

blocks.h2: 04 · SAN, iSCSI, Fibre Channel and CSI
paras: The note maps iSCSI / Fibre Channel storage networks to CSI (Container Storage Interface) . They address different layers: iSCSI carries SCSI over TCP/IP; Fibre Channel provides a dedicated storage transport; HBAs connect hosts to storage fabrics. CSI is a standardized interface by which container orchestrators request provisioning, attachment and mounting through storage drivers.

Application in Pod → filesystem → PersistentVolumeClaim → Kubernetes CSI driver → storage provisioner → block/file storage backend → (possibly iSCSI / FC / NVMe-oF / NFS / cloud storage) → physical disks / SSDs Correction: CSI is not a SAN controller or a replacement for Fibre Channel. It integrates Kubernetes with whichever storage backend the CSI driver supports.

Guided: copper twisted pair, coaxial and fiber constrain signal propagation along a material path. Unguided: radio and other wireless electromagnetic propagation use space as the transmission medium. Virtual: VLANs, VRFs, tunnels, VXLAN overlays, veth pairs, Linux bridges, virtual switches, VPNs and software-defined policies are logical constructs implemented on physical hardware and links.

VLANs segment Layer-2 broadcast domains; VRFs isolate routing tables; VPNs can provide protected tunnels; VXLAN encapsulates L2 segments over an L3 underlay; LAG bonds links into one logical aggregation; SSIDs identify Wi-Fi networks, but SSIDs alone do not guarantee isolation.

blocks.h2: 06 · Trace a packet: laptop to application Pod
paras: Laptop app creates HTTPS request → OS TCP/IP stack → laptop Wi-Fi NIC → radio frames → AP → access switch → distribution/core → firewall → edge router → ISP → Internet → public load balancer → Gateway/Ingress → Service backend selection → worker-node NIC → CNI datapath → Pod eth0 → socket → application process At each hop, distinguish physical signal , link-layer framing , IP forwarding , transport connection , TLS security , and application request . A Service can use iptables, IPVS or eBPF depending on cluster configuration; not every packet necessarily passes through every named component.

Connect this chapter to Chapter 03 (silicon/NIC), Chapter 10 (storage/memory), Chapter 11 (interfaces, networking), and Chapter 12 (source-by-source review). Suggested lab sequence: inspect ip link and ip route on Linux; create two namespaces and a veth pair; configure a Linux bridge; deploy two Pods and a ClusterIP Service; inspect CNI and NetworkPolicy behavior; trace an HTTPS request through an Ingress; provision a PVC using a CSI driver.

Verification checklist: Identify the actual CNI and its policy capabilities; whether kube-proxy is enabled; the physical network underlay; ingress/Gateway controller; firewall placement; CSI driver and backing storage; HA and failover domains. Do not infer these from Kubernetes alone.

tables.h2: 02 · Kubernetes network path and exact analogies
rows: Notebook analogy
Engineering interpretation
What is NOT equivalent
Modem → Ingress / cloud gateway
Both may be near an entry boundary; Ingress/Gateway exposes and routes application traffic
Ingress does not convert DSL, optical, or radio physical signals
Firewall → NetworkPolicy / service mesh
NetworkPolicy controls selected pod traffic; meshes may add identity, mTLS and L7 authorization
Neither automatically replaces a perimeter NGFW; enforcement depends on implementation
Router → kube-proxy / CNI routing
CNI-provisioned routes, kernel forwarding and kube-proxy/eBPF service translation can steer packets
kube-proxy is not a general WAN router; some clusters replace it with eBPF
Switch → Service / bridge
Linux bridges switch L2 frames; Services expose stable L4 virtual destinations
Service is not an Ethernet switch; ClusterIP is not inherently a load balancer for all protocols
NIC → eth0 inside Pod
Pod interfaces are commonly veth-backed and connected through host networking
eth0 in a Pod is usually virtual, not a dedicated physical NIC
Physical media → overlay VXLAN
Overlays encapsulate traffic over an underlay built from real NICs, switches and links
VXLAN is optional; not every CNI uses it
VLAN → namespace
Both help organize boundaries
Namespace alone does not isolate network traffic; use policies, routes and security controls
LAG → ReplicaSet / Service
Both are used in broader resilience/capacity discussions
ReplicaSets scale pod replicas, not bandwidth of a physical link
